To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) World Bank projects are more likely to be implemented at the local level in countries with lower levels of government transparency, and 2) World Bank projects implemented at the local rather than the national level are more likely to have a positive impact in terms of the number of people reached.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether the World Bank’s allocation of project implementation power to recipient countries is influenced by the level of transparency of the latter.
how the World Bank allocates its implementing power, and how the level of implementation is affected by the relative importance and availability of local information.
how information asymmetry affects the choice of implementing level in the context of development aid.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our results suggest that the allocation of implementing power to local levels of government may be an efficient way to reduce information asymmetry and to improve the effectiveness of aid.
the World Bank allocates implementing power based on the level of local information, and that the allocation process is influenced by transparency.
the World Bank does seem to take into account the relative importance of information at the recipient level, and that this has an impact on the allocation of implementing power.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, when the level of transparency is low, the probability that a local level project will be implemented is higher, while, when the level is high, the probability that the project will be implemented at a national level is higher.
the allocation of implementing power is influenced by the degree of transparency at the recipient country.
transparency does matter for the allocation of implementing power, and that the World Bank is sensitive to the importance of local information in this allocation process.
The main takeaway from our work is that
transparency matters for the choice of implementing power.
the World Bank’s choice to implement projects locally rather than nationally can be interpreted as a way to mitigate the informational asymmetry between the national and the local level.
the allocation of implementation power is not only determined by the relative importance and efficiency of local information, but also by the transparency level at the country level.
